title: How To Handle Students Who Give You Attitude https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/03/04/how-to-handle-students-who-give-you-attitude/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes between blatant disrespect, which requires a consequence, and minor "attitude" — eye rolls, sighs, sarcastic remarks — which he argues is better handled without invoking the classroom management plan. He explains that attitude in response to a simple request is usually an act of personal frustration rather than an attack on the teacher, comparable to rolling your eyes at a DMV clerk who is only trying to help. Enforcing a consequence for it, he warns, tends to deepen the student's frustration rather than resolve it. Instead, he recommends responding with a brief, genuine smile or light chuckle that communicates understanding without mockery, then moving on without further comment. Over time, using this as a default response reduces classroom tension, increases students' willingness to follow directions, and replaces attitude with acceptance and even shared laughter. The article stresses the importance of distinguishing this pattern from true disrespect, which still warrants a consequence.
points: Minor attitude — eye rolls, sighs, sarcasm — is usually personal frustration, not disrespect directed at the teacher.
Enforcing a consequence for simple attitude tends to deepen a student's frustration rather than resolve it.
A brief, genuine smile or light chuckle in response to attitude diffuses tension better than lecturing or arguing.
Using this response consistently, as a default, reduces classroom tension and increases students' eagerness to comply.
Teachers must still distinguish attitude from blatant disrespect, which requires a consequence under the classroom management plan.
quotes: They're responses to teacher requests or reminders (i.e. 'Please put your backpack away.') that aren't quite disrespectful. But darn close.
For one, I don’t believe it rises to the level of disrespect. Although it often feels like it, it isn’t directed at you.
Enforcing a consequence, then, often makes things worse, deepening the student’s frustration and discontent.
The way it works is when a student rolls their eyes or gives attitude about something you've said, you're going to smile at them.
It communicates that you don’t give directions because you like bossing people around—which, based on their experience in the past, is how many students view teachers.
The only danger is to be sure you’re clear on the difference between a student having a bad moment and blatant disrespect, which must always be followed by a consequence.
In time, you'll eliminate virtually all 'attitude' from your classroom. And replace it with acceptance, eagerness, and smiles.
